body_markdown:
*Wait, Tom!* You may be thinking. *What in the world is this? It’s not an Electra 225 Limited, a Town Car, a Fleetwood Talisman—not even a downsized ’82 Bonneville Model G Brougham!* Well, I know it may be hard to believe, but I do like some other cars. Really!


A casual glance at[my Hagerty articles](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/) may suggest otherwise, but I do like some classic cars that are less than 20 feet long, sans vinyl roofs, opera windows, opera lamps, and Firemist or Diamond Fire paint. In fact, today’s subject may be my least[“Broughamy”](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/klockau-classics/1976-cadillac-fleetwood-red-white-and-brougham/comment-page-2/) subject ever.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


I mean, look at this, my friends. Was there ever a less-Broughamy interior, ever? The cabin of this Volkswagen Thing is, somehow, even more severe than that of a WWII Jeep. No leather-wrapped wheel. No Carpathian-grain wood trim. No cruise control, no Twilight Sentinel, no deluxe Tampico carpeting. No leather, no 16-way power seat. But still, isn’t it cool?


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Originally known as the Type 181, this odd-looking VW was a kind of reincarnation of the wartime Kubelwagen. First introduced in 1969 as a proposed all-purpose military vehicle, it was of course heavily based on the evergreen Type 1 “Beetle.”


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


It was[initially developed for the military](https://www.hagerty.com/media/lists/8-rugged-classics-with-military-origins-you-should-know/) , but later on was sold in Germany and England as a “fun-type” civilian car. When production was extended to Mexican VW factories, it was finally introduced to North America as “the Thing.”


Thomas Klockau


It first appeared in 1973 in the USA. Riding atop the somewhat wider chassis of the[Karmann-Ghia](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/the-secret-agent-who-created-the-karmann-ghia/) , most of its underpinnings came from the Beetle, right down to the 46-hp four-cylinder engine under the rear engine lid, identical to the version in the civilian Beetle.


Thomas Klockau


And while the go-anywhere do-anything marketing implied otherwise, these were not four-wheel-drive, just RWD.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


As the brochure told prospects, “Our Thing does Your Thing. Whatever your thing may be.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


“Well, we’ve got just the thing. The Thing. With back seats that fold down for extra storage space. Removable top and doors, and a windshield that snaps down for dune buggy fun.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


“A double-jointed rear axle to keep the wheels in contact with the ground, even over the toughest terrain. Four-wheel independent suspension to smooth out the bumps. High ground clearance and special protection for rough terrain use.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


“The Thing offers all this, plus gas economy: 21 miles per gallon. And that is some thing.”


Thomas Klockau


Despite all the hype, the Thing was only offered in the USA for 1973 and 1974. More stringent passenger-car safety standards pushed it out of our market starting in 1975, though the model remained in production in other countries through 1980.


Thomas Klockau


But they’re cool, as long as you’re into maximum utility and minimal frills. I just like them. Though I own a Cadillac and a Lincoln, I still think they’re cool.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Only three colors were offered in 1973 for U.S. models: Sunshine Yellow, Blizzard White, and our featured car’s color, and my preferred hue, Pumpkin Orange. There was also an available “Acapulco Thing” in a two-tone blue and white color combo. That version included a festive striped “Surrey Top.”


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


You don’t see as many of these as Beetles, due to the admittedly short U.S. production run. But they are *very* well-loved by their owners today. Who doesn’t want some Thing fun?


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)
